performers: Czech National Symphony Orchestra, as the Musopen Symphony Orchestra
intro: “In the Hall of the Mountain King”, the fourth movement of the Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, Op. 46, depicts the troll king’s hall from Ibsen’s Peer Gynt, and its single four-bar tune is repeated and quickened until the whole orchestra plays it. The Czech National Symphony Orchestra performs it for the Musopen project.

sections.label: A″ · Più vivo, fortissimo
sections.mNote: Faster and louder through to the end.

cues.title: Opening theme
cues.text: A four-bar theme enters, marked pp and e sempre staccato. It rises by step from B to F♯, falls to D and rises to F♯ again, and the second bar alternates between E♯ and E natural. The four bars then repeat several times.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, “In the Hall of the Mountain King”, opening bars (B minor, “Alla marcia molto marcato”, pp, e sempre staccato), in the piano version after The University Society edition (1918), typeset for the Mutopia Project: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/GriegE/O46/Dans_l_antre_du_roi_de_la_montagne/Dans_l_antre_du_roi_de_la_montagne.ly
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Frants Beyer, 1874
cues.text: In August 1874 Grieg told his friend Frants Beyer that he had written a piece for the troll king’s hall that he could not bear to hear, because it reeked “of cow-pats, of Norwegian-Norwegianness and smugness”. He hoped the irony would come through.
cues.evidence: Grieg to Frants Beyer, August 1874, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon, “Edvard Grieg” (“som jeg bogstavelig ikke kan tåle at høre på, således klinger det af Kokager, af Norsk-norskhed og Sigselvnokhed”, translated here): https://nbl.snl.no/Edvard_Grieg

cues.title: Più vivo, closing section
cues.text: At Più vivo the dynamic is fortissimo, and Grieg marks sempre stretto sin al fine (pressing on to the end). The tune is unchanged. George Bernard Shaw heard it in London in 1889 and called it “a riotous piece of weird fun”.
cues.evidence: Grieg, “In the Hall of the Mountain King”, piano version after The University Society edition (1918), Mutopia Project: Più vivo, ff, and “sempre stretto sin al fine”: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/GriegE/O46/Dans_l_antre_du_roi_de_la_montagne/Dans_l_antre_du_roi_de_la_montagne.ly. John Henken, Hollywood Bowl programme note: Shaw’s review of an 1889 London performance, “a riotous piece of weird fun”: https://www.hollywoodbowl.com/musicdb/pieces/2684/peer-gynt-suite-no-1-op-46

composer.epithet: Composer, the son of a Bergen merchant, who used Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party in concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. In his essay Min første Succes he recalled the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, but he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
